messages.content: I want to develop an open-world visual recognizer that can distinguish novel classes from domain shifts while learning new classes without forgetting. What does that goal require?

It has two connected parts. The recognizer needs to recognize when an input belongs to a novel class, without treating a domain-shifted example of a known class as novel merely because it looks different. It also needs to learn classes as they are added while preserving its ability to recognize the classes it already knew. The stated targets make both parts measurable.
What are the targets for distinguishing novelty from domain shift?

The target is at least 80% novel-class recall while keeping false rejection of domain-shifted known classes at no more than 5%. Both conditions matter together: finding novel classes is not enough if the recognizer also rejects too many shifted examples of known classes.
So a domain-shifted known-class example should still count as known, even if it appears different?

Yes. In this goal, a domain shift changes the appearance or conditions under which a known class is seen; it does not, by itself, make that class novel. The distinction the recognizer must make is between a genuinely novel class and a changed presentation of one it already knows.
What exactly does the 5% limit refer to?

It limits false rejection of domain-shifted known classes to at most 5%. In other words, among the shifted examples that are still from known classes, the recognizer should not incorrectly reject more than that limit as outside its known classes. It is a constraint alongside the novel-class recall target, not a substitute for it.
And novel-class recall of at least 80% means it has to catch most genuinely new classes?

It means the target recall for novel-class examples is at least 80%: the recognizer should identify at least that proportion as novel under the stated condition on false rejection. The goal does not specify a finer-grained scoring rule for identifying which new class each example belongs to at that stage.
Could it meet the goal by marking almost everything as novel?

Not if doing so pushes false rejection of domain-shifted known classes above 5%. That limit is what prevents high novel-class recall from being achieved simply by rejecting known-class examples indiscriminately. The intended outcome is to distinguish the two cases, not to favor one by ignoring the other.
What is the separate target for learning new classes without forgetting?

After ten class additions, the recognizer should retain at least 95% of its initial known-class accuracy and achieve at least 70% added-class accuracy. The first threshold concerns performance on the original known classes relative to its initial accuracy; the second concerns performance on the added classes after those ten additions.
Does “retain at least 95% of its initial known-class accuracy” mean known-class accuracy must be at least 95% in absolute terms?

No. As written, the retention target is relative to the initial known-class accuracy: at least 95% of that initial level must remain after ten class additions. It does not state an absolute 95% accuracy requirement for the known classes.
Why is there also an added-class accuracy threshold?

Preserving performance on the original known classes would not, by itself, show that the recognizer learned the additions. The at-least-70% added-class accuracy target addresses that other side of the goal. After ten class additions, it needs both sufficient retention of initial known-class accuracy and sufficient accuracy on the added classes.
Does the goal require the retention threshold after every individual addition?

The stated checkpoint is after ten class additions. It does not give a separate numerical retention target after each intermediate addition. The broader aim is to learn without forgetting, but the explicit accuracy requirements are tied to the point after ten additions.
Is the 70% requirement stated for every added class separately?

The wording specifies at least 70% added-class accuracy after ten class additions. It does not specify a separate minimum for each added class or how accuracy across the added classes is aggregated. Those details should not be assumed from the target alone.
How do the novelty and learning parts fit together conceptually?

They describe two challenges for the same open-world recognizer. When it encounters something unfamiliar, it must distinguish a novel class from a domain-shifted known class. As classes are subsequently added, it must learn them without losing too much accuracy on the initially known classes. The novelty and false-rejection thresholds describe the distinction; the post-addition accuracy thresholds describe learning and retention.
Does calling something novel already mean the system has learned to recognize it as an added class?

No. Identifying an example as belonging to a novel class is distinct from accurately recognizing classes after they have been added. The goal includes both abilities, but its 80% novel-class recall target should not be conflated with its 70% added-class accuracy target.
If the recognizer meets the added-class accuracy target but loses too much of its original known-class accuracy, would that satisfy the goal?

No. After ten class additions, it must meet both requirements: at least 70% added-class accuracy and retention of at least 95% of its initial known-class accuracy. Good performance on the additions does not remove the retention requirement.
Likewise, could strong retention compensate for missing the novel-class recall target?

No. The stated goals address different aspects of open-world recognition, and no compensation between their thresholds is specified. Retaining known-class accuracy after additions does not replace the requirement for at least 80% novel-class recall at no more than 5% false rejection of domain-shifted known classes.
Can you put the complete objective into one precise statement without adding an evaluation procedure?

Develop an open-world visual recognizer that distinguishes genuinely novel classes from domain-shifted known classes and learns new classes without forgetting. Target at least 80% novel-class recall with no more than 5% false rejection of domain-shifted known classes; after ten class additions, retain at least 95% of the initial known-class accuracy and achieve at least 70% added-class accuracy. The goal states those outcomes, but it does not prescribe a particular method or evaluation procedure.

For the open-world recognizer, I propose calibrating frozen CLIP prototype novelty scores on shifted known images, then learning new classes with replay-trained adapters and logit distillation. How do those pieces address the goal?

The proposal gives each part of the goal a role. Frozen CLIP prototype novelty scores provide a basis for assessing whether an image appears to belong to a known class or might be novel. Calibrating those scores on shifted known images is meant to help avoid mistaking a changed presentation of a known class for a novel class. Replay-trained adapters and logit distillation address the learning side: they are proposed ways to incorporate added classes while preserving earlier recognition behavior. These are proposed mechanisms, not evidence yet that the numerical targets are met.
What does “frozen CLIP” mean in the novelty-scoring part?

It means the CLIP component used for those prototype novelty scores remains fixed rather than being updated as part of that scoring approach. The proposal does not say that every component of the recognizer is frozen: it separately calls for adapters to be trained when learning new classes.
And what is the role of a prototype in that phrase?

A prototype serves as a representative reference for a class when interpreting an image's relationship to known classes. The proposal uses CLIP prototype novelty scores for that comparison. It does not specify how the prototypes are constructed, how many there are per class, or an exact formula for the novelty score.
Is a high novelty score necessarily a novel class?

Not necessarily. A domain-shifted image of a known class might look unusual relative to a prototype too. That is why the proposal specifically calls for calibrating the novelty scores on shifted known images: an unusual score should be interpreted with that known-class variation in mind. The proposal does not state a particular cutoff or decision rule.
Why calibrate on shifted known images rather than just use the prototype scores as they come?

The distinction in the goal is not simply between familiar-looking and unfamiliar-looking images. Some images can look different because of domain shift while still belonging to known classes. Calibrating on shifted known images is intended to make the interpretation of the novelty scores sensitive to that possibility, rather than treating every departure from the familiar appearance as evidence of a new class.
Does the proposal specify exactly how the calibration works?

No. It identifies what is calibrated—the frozen CLIP prototype novelty scores—and the kind of images used for calibration—shifted known images. It does not give a calibration algorithm, a score transformation, a threshold-selection rule, or a claim about measured performance.
Should I read “calibrate on shifted known images” as saying novel examples are available for calibration too?
No. The proposal specifically names shifted known images as the calibration basis. It does not state whether novel examples are available for calibration, so their availability should not be assumed.
How does this connect to the target of at least 80% novel-class recall with at most 5% false rejection of domain-shifted known classes?

That target describes what the novelty decision ultimately needs to achieve. The proposed calibration addresses a particular risk for the 5% limit: shifted known images being incorrectly rejected as novel. It must also leave room to identify genuinely novel classes to reach at least 80% recall. The proposal alone does not establish that either threshold, or both together, will be achieved.
Now explain the learning part. What are replay-trained adapters doing in this proposal?

They are the proposed trainable component for learning new classes. “Replay-trained” indicates that replay is used in training the adapters, so learning the additions is not considered in isolation from earlier recognition. The proposal does not specify the adapters' architecture, what is replayed, or a replay schedule.
Is training adapters inconsistent with keeping CLIP frozen?

No. Those statements concern different components. CLIP is frozen for the prototype novelty-scoring approach, while the adapters are trained to learn new classes. The proposal does not specify every interaction between those components, but training an adapter does not by itself mean updating the frozen CLIP component.
What does logit distillation add alongside replay?

Logit distillation uses output scores, or logits, as guidance during learning. In this proposal, it is paired with replay-trained adapters to help preserve recognition behavior while new classes are learned. The statement does not specify where the reference logits come from, how they are compared, or how strongly distillation is weighted.
So replay and logit distillation both relate to forgetting, but they aren't interchangeable terms?

Right. Replay refers to bringing earlier material back into the training process; logit distillation refers to guidance from output scores. The proposal includes both for learning new classes without forgetting. It does not say that either one alone is sufficient, or quantify how much each contributes.
Does it say what happens to the prototypes when new classes are added?

No. The proposal names frozen CLIP prototype novelty scores for novelty assessment and replay-trained adapters with logit distillation for learning new classes. It does not specify whether or how prototypes are created or changed for added classes.
Do I need to assume a particular order, such as completing all calibration before any adapter training?

The proposal identifies the two activities and their purposes, but does not lay out a detailed sequence or dependency between them. You can describe calibration as part of the novelty distinction and adapter training with distillation as part of class addition without asserting a specific training order.
How should I relate the learning proposal to the after-ten-additions accuracy requirements?

Replay-trained adapters and logit distillation are proposed means of pursuing those requirements. After ten class additions, the goal is to retain at least 95% of the initial known-class accuracy and achieve at least 70% added-class accuracy. The proposal does not report either accuracy, so it should not be described as already satisfying those targets.
Can you summarize the proposal precisely without making it sound like a completed experiment?

Use frozen CLIP prototype novelty scores and calibrate them on shifted known images to support the distinction between novel classes and domain-shifted known classes. For class additions, train adapters with replay and use logit distillation to support learning while limiting forgetting. This is a proposed approach to the open-world recognizer goal; its ability to meet the stated recall, false-rejection, and post-addition accuracy thresholds remains unestablished.
Can shift-calibrated CLIP prototypes prevent weather-induced false novelty without masking unseen classes?

That is the key question, not an established outcome of the proposal. Weather can change how an image of a known class appears, so calibration on shifted known images could help keep such images from being mistaken for novel classes. But calibration must not make the recognizer so willing to accept unusual images as known that it also accepts images from genuinely unseen classes. Whether it can do both has not been established.
What does “weather-induced false novelty” mean here?

It means incorrectly treating an image as evidence of a novel class when it actually depicts a known class whose appearance has changed under weather conditions. The novelty judgment would be false because the class is still known; the weather is a shift in its presentation, not a new class.
Would shift calibration be intended to make the prototype scores less sensitive to weather?

It would be intended to prevent differences caused by domain shift from being interpreted automatically as novelty. That does not necessarily mean making the scores insensitive to every change. The important distinction is whether the recognizer can tolerate weather-related variation in known classes while still responding to differences that indicate an unseen class.
Why might those two aims conflict?

Both a weather-shifted known image and an unseen-class image might appear atypical relative to known-class prototypes. If calibration broadly treats atypical scores as acceptable for known classes, it could reduce false novelty from weather but also mask genuinely unseen classes. If it remains too strict, it might detect unseen classes while continuing to reject weather-shifted known ones. The question is whether the distinction can be preserved rather than merely moving errors from one side to the other.
Does calibrating on shifted known images prove the method can separate those cases?

No. Shifted known images provide information about how known classes can appear under shift. They do not, by themselves, establish how unseen classes will score or whether those scores will remain distinguishable. Calibration is a proposed response to false novelty, not proof that unseen classes remain detectable.
Is weather necessarily one of the shifts represented by those calibration images?

That is not specified. The proposal says to calibrate frozen CLIP prototype novelty scores on shifted known images; it does not describe which shifts those images contain. So the weather-specific question cannot be answered by assuming that weather is represented in calibration.
If weather is represented, is that enough to answer yes?

Not on its own. Even if shifted known images include weather-related variation, that would only speak to part of the question. The recognizer would still need to avoid masking unseen classes. The presence of weather-shifted known images in calibration would not, by itself, establish that both aims are met.
And if weather is not represented, can we conclude calibration will fail?

No. The proposal does not provide enough information to conclude either failure or success in that case. The careful statement is that its ability to prevent weather-induced false novelty would be uncertain, and its effect on unseen-class detection would also remain uncertain.
Is “masking unseen classes” the opposite error from weather-induced false novelty?

In this context, yes. Weather-induced false novelty means rejecting a weather-shifted example of a known class as novel. Masking an unseen class means treating a genuinely novel-class example as if it belonged among known classes. One error overcalls novelty; the other overlooks it.
How does this question relate to the recognizer's numerical targets?

It probes whether the proposed novelty approach can satisfy both sides of the target together: at least 80% novel-class recall and no more than 5% false rejection of domain-shifted known classes. Avoiding weather-induced false novelty bears on the false-rejection side when weather shifts known-class images. Avoiding the masking of unseen classes bears on novel-class recall. No result has been given showing that shift-calibrated CLIP prototypes meet either threshold.
Could the weather problem be considered solved if false rejection of shifted known classes stays low?

That would address only one side. A low false-rejection rate for shifted known classes is valuable, but the question explicitly asks whether that can happen without masking unseen classes. If unseen-class examples are routinely accepted as known, reducing weather-induced false novelty would not resolve the full distinction.
Does keeping CLIP frozen itself guarantee that unseen classes will remain visible to the novelty scores?

No. “Frozen” means the CLIP component used for prototype novelty scoring is not updated in that proposal. It does not guarantee how its scores will behave for weather-shifted known classes or unseen classes, and it does not remove the need to examine what calibration does to their interpretation.
So is the question really about the prototypes, or about their calibration?

It concerns the combination: CLIP prototype novelty scores as the basis for comparison, and shift calibration as the proposed way to interpret those scores in the presence of shifted known images. The central uncertainty is whether that calibrated interpretation can reduce weather-induced false novelty while retaining sensitivity to unseen classes.
Can you give a simple conceptual example without assuming any measured behavior?

Consider two hypothetical images that look unusual relative to known-class prototypes. One is a known class seen under different weather; the other belongs to an unseen class. A successful distinction would keep the first from being rejected solely because of the weather while still recognizing the second as novel. This illustrates the question; it does not claim the proposed scores actually separate the two.
Would eliminating all weather-related rejections be the right interpretation of “prevent weather-induced false novelty”?

The question asks whether calibration can prevent false novelty caused by weather without masking unseen classes. It does not specify a separate zero-error requirement or claim that every weather-affected image must be accepted. The existing goal sets a limit of no more than 5% false rejection for domain-shifted known classes, alongside the novel-class recall target.
What can we say confidently at this point?

We can state the proposed mechanism and the unresolved issue: shift calibration of frozen CLIP prototype novelty scores is meant to help distinguish shifted known images from novel classes, but it is not yet established whether it prevents weather-induced false novelty while preserving recognition of unseen classes. Neither success nor failure on that weather-specific tradeoff follows from the proposal alone.

I have a more specific hypothesis for the weather question: on WeatherShift-10, shift-calibrated prototypes will achieve at least 80% novel recall at no more than 5% shifted-known false rejection, outperforming global CLIP thresholds. Is that a fair statement?

Yes, as a hypothesis. It predicts that, on WeatherShift-10, shift-calibrated prototypes will reach both thresholds together—at least 80% novel recall and at most 5% false rejection of shifted-known examples—and will outperform global CLIP thresholds. It does not report that any of those outcomes have already been observed.
How does that address the question about weather-induced false novelty without masking unseen classes?

The shifted-known false-rejection limit addresses the risk of treating a known class under shift as novel. The novel-recall target addresses the opposite risk: failing to recognize genuinely novel classes. Predicting both on WeatherShift-10 makes the tradeoff in that question explicit, rather than focusing only on reducing false novelty.
Does the hypothesis say that the recognizer will never reject a weather-shifted known image?

No. Its stated limit is no more than 5% shifted-known false rejection on WeatherShift-10, not zero false rejection. Nor does it say that every unseen-class example will be recognized as novel; the predicted novel recall is at least 80%.
When I say “at least 80% novel recall at no more than 5% shifted-known false rejection,” are those separate predictions or a joint condition?

They form a joint condition. The hypothesis predicts at least 80% novel recall while shifted-known false rejection is no higher than 5%. Reaching the recall figure only by rejecting too many shifted-known examples would not satisfy that wording.
Could a very permissive novelty decision satisfy the false-rejection limit while masking unseen classes?

Conceptually, yes: accepting unusual images as known could keep shifted-known false rejection low but also cause novel examples to be overlooked. The at-least-80% novel-recall requirement prevents that from counting as success for this hypothesis. The hypothesis predicts that shift-calibrated prototypes can satisfy both requirements, rather than merely favoring one.
What is being compared when I say they will outperform global CLIP thresholds?

The comparison is between shift-calibrated prototypes and global CLIP thresholds. “Outperforming” is part of the predicted result, not a finding. The statement does not specify a numerical margin, a particular performance summary for the comparison, or the observed results of either approach.
Does outperforming global CLIP thresholds mean the calibrated prototypes must have both higher novel recall and lower shifted-known false rejection?

The hypothesis does not specify that stronger, metric-by-metric claim. It predicts that the calibrated prototypes will outperform global CLIP thresholds while meeting the stated joint recall and false-rejection condition. Without a more precise definition of “outperform,” we should not add a requirement that each individual measure improves over the comparison.
Are the global CLIP thresholds the same thing as the shift-calibrated prototypes?

No. They are named as the comparison baseline, while shift-calibrated prototypes are the approach the hypothesis expects to do better. The hypothesis does not provide their exact scoring rules or how either is configured, so the distinction should stay at that level.
Does the hypothesis specify how much calibration helps?

No. It specifies the predicted thresholds for shift-calibrated prototypes and a predicted advantage over global CLIP thresholds, but not the size of that advantage or a measured change caused by calibration.
What exactly can I infer from the name WeatherShift-10?

Here, WeatherShift-10 names the setting on which the prediction is made. The hypothesis does not describe its classes, the kinds of weather involved, its size, or how examples are divided. Those details should not be inferred from the name alone.
Is this prediction meant to apply to every possible domain shift?

No. The hypothesis explicitly names WeatherShift-10. It should not be extended to every domain shift or every collection of unseen classes without additional information. The broader open-world goal provides context, but this prediction has the stated scope.
Can I treat shifted-known false rejection as a measure of weather-induced false novelty here?

It captures the relevant kind of error for this weather-focused hypothesis: shifted-known examples are incorrectly rejected as novel. The wording does not define further subcategories of errors or specify how particular weather conditions are represented, so it is safest to stay with the stated shifted-known false-rejection measure on WeatherShift-10.
Does this hypothesis also predict the outcome after ten class additions?

No. It concerns novel recall, shifted-known false rejection, and the comparison with global CLIP thresholds on WeatherShift-10. It does not predict the post-addition known-class or added-class accuracies. Those remain separate requirements of the broader goal, not additional results implied by this hypothesis.
Is there any result here that supports saying the calibration already prevents weather-induced false novelty?

No result is stated here. The claim is forward-looking: shift-calibrated prototypes *will* meet the specified joint thresholds on WeatherShift-10 and outperform global CLIP thresholds. Until an outcome is supplied, it should remain a prediction rather than a demonstrated prevention of false novelty.
What would be inaccurate about shortening it to “calibrated prototypes solve weather shift”?

That would overstate both the certainty and the scope. The node is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated solution, and it makes a specific prediction on WeatherShift-10: at least 80% novel recall at no more than 5% shifted-known false rejection, with performance exceeding global CLIP thresholds. “Solve weather shift” leaves out those limits and could imply broader, completed success.
Then how would you state it concisely while preserving the comparison?

The hypothesis is that, on WeatherShift-10, shift-calibrated prototypes will achieve at least 80% novel recall with no more than 5% shifted-known false rejection, outperforming global CLIP thresholds. That wording preserves the joint condition, the comparison, and the fact that this is a prediction.

To examine the weather-shift question, I plan to calibrate on shifted-known validation images, then compare WeatherShift-10 novel recall against global CLIP thresholds at 5% false rejection. Does that state the plan clearly?

Yes. The plan is to use shifted-known validation images for calibration and compare novel recall on WeatherShift-10 with the recall obtained using global CLIP thresholds, with the comparison made at 5% false rejection. It describes what you intend to do, not an observed result.
Why use shifted-known validation images for calibration?

They provide examples of classes that remain known despite a shift in appearance. Calibrating with them is intended to inform how the CLIP prototype novelty scores are interpreted when a known-class image looks unusual. The plan does not specify the calibration calculation or establish that calibration will work.
Does “shifted-known” mean those images should be treated as novel during calibration?
No. They are shifted examples of known classes. The point is to account for their changed appearance without confusing the change itself with evidence of a novel class.
What is the purpose of specifying validation images?

It identifies the images used for the calibration step: shifted-known validation images. The plan does not say how those images were collected or divided, nor does it specify any other calibration inputs.
Am I also saying that I will calibrate on novel images?

No. The calibration input named in this plan is shifted-known validation images. The plan separately calls for comparing novel recall on WeatherShift-10; it does not say that novel images are used to calibrate the scores.
What does novel recall tell us in this comparison?

It concerns the proportion of genuinely novel examples identified as novel. Comparing it on WeatherShift-10 asks whether the calibrated approach continues to recognize unseen classes when false rejection is held to the stated 5% condition. Novel recall alone would not describe what happens to shifted-known examples, which is why the false-rejection condition matters.
Why make the comparison at 5% false rejection rather than compare recall without mentioning false rejection?

A novelty decision can appear better at catching unseen classes simply because it rejects more images, including shifted examples of known classes. Specifying 5% false rejection makes the cost to shifted-known recognition part of the comparison. The plan is about novel recall under that condition, not recall considered in isolation.
Does the 5% figure refer to false rejection of unseen classes?

No. False rejection here concerns shifted-known images being rejected as though they were novel. Unseen classes are the subject of the novel-recall measure. Those two measures capture the opposing errors raised by the weather-shift question.
Should I interpret “at 5% false rejection” as a result that has already been measured?
No. It states the operating condition for the planned comparison. The plan supplies no measured false-rejection rate or novel-recall value.
What is the comparison approach?

Global CLIP thresholds are the comparison approach. The plan is to compare WeatherShift-10 novel recall for the shift-calibrated prototype approach against novel recall using those global thresholds at the stated false-rejection condition. It does not define the global thresholds or give their performance.
Does the plan specify that the calibrated approach will have higher recall?
No. It specifies a comparison, not its outcome. The recall could only be described as higher, lower, or equal once results are available; none are supplied in this plan.
What if I simply compare the two approaches at different false-rejection rates?

That would not express the comparison stated here. The plan calls for comparing WeatherShift-10 novel recall against global CLIP thresholds at 5% false rejection. Keeping that condition in view is important because otherwise differences in recall could reflect different willingness to reject shifted-known images.
Does this plan tell us how to set a threshold to reach the 5% condition?

No. It specifies calibration on shifted-known validation images and a comparison at 5% false rejection, but not a threshold-setting rule or the exact form of the calibrated scores. Those details should not be presented as decisions already made.
Does it say whether WeatherShift-10 provides the validation images?
It does not say. The plan names shifted-known validation images for calibration and WeatherShift-10 for the novel-recall comparison, without specifying their relationship beyond those roles.
Is this also a plan to evaluate replay-trained adapters or logit distillation?

No. Those belong to the proposed new-class learning component. This plan is focused on calibration and the novelty comparison: shifted-known validation images, WeatherShift-10 novel recall, global CLIP thresholds, and the 5% false-rejection condition. It does not specify an evaluation of class additions or forgetting.
How directly does this plan address the possibility of masking unseen classes?

By comparing novel recall after calibration at the specified false-rejection condition. If calibration makes shifted-known images less likely to be falsely rejected but also causes unseen classes to be treated as known, novel recall would reflect that loss of sensitivity. The plan sets up that comparison; it does not tell us what the recall will be.
And how directly does it address false novelty caused by weather?

The shifted-known images used for calibration and the 5% false-rejection condition address the risk of rejecting known classes under shift. The plan does not specify which shifts are represented in the validation images or provide a measured weather-specific error rate, so it should not be described as already preventing weather-induced false novelty.
Can you phrase the plan in one sentence, keeping the calibration data, comparison, setting, and condition explicit?

Calibrate the CLIP prototype novelty scores on shifted-known validation images, then compare novel recall on WeatherShift-10 with that of global CLIP thresholds at 5% false rejection of shifted-known images.

The activity is to evaluate calibrated prototypes against global CLIP thresholds on held-out WeatherShift-10 weather, reporting novel recall at 5% shifted-known false rejection. What does that evaluation establish?

It sets up a comparison, but it does not yet establish an outcome. On held-out WeatherShift-10 weather, the evaluation will compare how well calibrated prototypes and global CLIP thresholds identify novel examples when shifted-known false rejection is at 5%. Reporting novel recall under that condition makes the ability to detect novelty interpretable alongside the risk of falsely rejecting shifted known classes.
What does “held-out weather” add to the activity?

It specifies that the WeatherShift-10 weather used for this evaluation is held out, rather than simply describing a comparison on WeatherShift-10 without that qualification. The activity does not identify the weather conditions, the size of the held-out portion, or the details of how it was held out.
Should I say the prototypes are calibrated on that held-out weather?

No. This activity says to evaluate calibrated prototypes on held-out WeatherShift-10 weather. It does not say to calibrate them on that weather. The distinction between calibration and the held-out evaluation should remain clear.
What is the baseline in the comparison?

Global CLIP thresholds are the comparison baseline. The activity calls for evaluating calibrated prototypes against them; it does not specify how those thresholds are set or report how either approach performs.
Why report novel recall at 5% shifted-known false rejection instead of just reporting novel recall?

Because novel recall can change with how readily a recognizer rejects images as novel. Stating the 5% shifted-known false-rejection condition keeps the cost of wrongly rejecting shifted examples of known classes visible in the comparison. The reported recall is therefore tied to that operating condition, rather than presented without context.
Does “shifted-known false rejection” refer to missing novel examples?

No. It refers to incorrectly rejecting examples that belong to known classes despite the shift. Missing genuinely novel examples affects novel recall. The activity considers novel recall at a specified level of the other error.
Are we reporting a single combined accuracy for known and novel classes?

No. The stated report is novel recall at 5% shifted-known false rejection. That preserves the distinction between detecting novel examples and avoiding false rejection of shifted-known ones; it does not define a combined accuracy measure.
Does the activity already tell us which approach has better novel recall?

No. It calls for an evaluation against global CLIP thresholds, but supplies no recall values or comparison result. Saying that calibrated prototypes outperform the thresholds at this stage would turn an intended comparison into an unsupported finding.
Is the 5% false-rejection figure an observed result in this description?
It is the specified condition for reporting novel recall, not a reported observation. The activity does not give a measured false-rejection rate or a measured novel-recall value.
Does this activity directly examine the concern that weather might make known classes look novel?

Yes, through its shifted-known false-rejection condition on held-out WeatherShift-10 weather. It also examines whether novel examples remain detectable by reporting novel recall under that condition. The activity is designed to make both sides of that concern visible, without presupposing the outcome.
How does it bear on the hypothesis about at least 80% novel recall?

The reported novel recall would provide a way to assess that predicted recall level while considering shifted-known false rejection. Comparing calibrated prototypes with global CLIP thresholds would also address the predicted comparison. This activity specifies what to evaluate and report; it does not state whether the prediction is borne out.
The hypothesis said no more than 5% false rejection, while the activity says recall at 5%. Should those phrases be treated as identical?

They are closely related but not identical wording. The activity specifies reporting novel recall at a 5% shifted-known false-rejection operating condition. The hypothesis predicts at least 80% novel recall with shifted-known false rejection no more than 5%. The activity should be described using its own stated condition, without claiming a measured rate or changing the hypothesis into a result.
Can we infer from this activity that performance will generalize to every weather condition?
No. Its stated scope is held-out WeatherShift-10 weather. It does not claim a result for every possible weather condition, and it does not supply results even for the held-out setting yet.
Does it say anything about learning ten additional classes or retaining initial known-class accuracy?

No. This activity is about the novelty comparison between calibrated prototypes and global CLIP thresholds on held-out WeatherShift-10 weather. It does not evaluate class additions, adapters, logit distillation, or post-addition accuracy.
What should the report make explicit so that the comparison is not misleading?

It should identify the two approaches—calibrated prototypes and global CLIP thresholds—the held-out WeatherShift-10 weather setting, and the reported measure: novel recall at 5% shifted-known false rejection. Those are the elements specified by the activity. No numerical recall or winner should be supplied without results.
Can you restate the activity without making it sound as though the evaluation has already succeeded?

Evaluate calibrated prototypes against global CLIP thresholds on held-out WeatherShift-10 weather, and report novel recall at 5% shifted-known false rejection. That states the activity and its reporting condition without asserting an outcome.
What did the held-out WeatherShift-10 evaluation show?

On held-out WeatherShift-10, calibrated prototypes achieved 83% novel recall at 5% shifted-known false rejection, versus 68% novel recall for global CLIP. The reported comparison favors the calibrated prototypes in that setting and at that false-rejection condition.
Can you unpack the 83% figure?

It is the reported novel recall for calibrated prototypes: 83% of novel examples were identified as novel in the held-out WeatherShift-10 evaluation at 5% shifted-known false rejection. It is a recall figure, not an overall accuracy figure.
